note: Final story. Numbers come from the real Trend Scanner output (scanner.json). Sources listed in docs/story.md.

steps.title: The lake we share
steps.text: Lake Erie provides drinking water for millions of people and supports fisheries and the regional economy (Canada–Ontario Lake Erie Action Plan). Every summer, algae blooms reach the beaches of our own city, Windsor.

steps.title: What the satellites saw
steps.text: NASA's MODIS-Aqua satellite measured chlorophyll-a, a sign of algae, over Lake Erie every bloom season (July to October) from 2003 to 2025. Our Trend Scanner found it rising about 1.55 mg/m³ per decade, a statistically significant trend (p < 0.001).

steps.title: Where it's changing
steps.text: Algae is rising in both the western basin (+1.34 mg/m³ per decade) and the central and eastern basins (+1.39), and both trends are significant. On the map, 1,300 of 1,593 satellite pixels show a significant increase and none show a decrease. Tap a square to see its numbers.

steps.title: Not every change is a trend
steps.text: Water temperature in the bloom season drifted up about 0.41 °C per decade from 2007 to 2025 (NOAA GLSEA satellite temperature), but the swings from year to year are larger, so it isn't a significant trend yet (p = 0.069). Our scanner says so instead of overclaiming.

steps.title: Why it matters for Windsor-Essex
steps.text: Blooms can affect drinking water and public health (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit). Some produce microcystin toxins that can harm people and animals (NOAA). They also affect beaches, tourism and recreation in the Essex region (Essex Region Conservation Authority). Note: satellite chlorophyll estimates how much algae there is, not how toxic it is.

steps.title: Explore it yourself
steps.text: Pick any variable in the Trend Scanner to see its chart, its trend in each basin, and its map. Then pick another Great Lake from the menu at the top: the same tool runs on all five. For the other lakes, the western and eastern sections split each lake at its middle, not at its basins.
